name: Public Key Infrastructure
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Machinery Behind Every Trusted Key
lesson.summary: Public key infrastructure is the full set of policies, roles, and systems, certificate authorities, registration processes, and revocation mechanisms, that make raw key pairs usable as verified real-world identities at scale.
lesson.body:
Key pair generation gives you a mathematical object: two related numbers, one you keep secret and one you can share freely. On its own, that object proves nothing about who created it or whether it should be trusted for anything in particular. Public key infrastructure, universally abbreviated PKI, is the name for everything built around raw key pairs to turn them into something a stranger can actually rely on: the certificate authorities, the procedures they follow, the software that checks certificates, and the mechanisms for handling keys that go bad. It is infrastructure in the same sense that roads and traffic lights are infrastructure for cars; the vehicle alone does not get you anywhere safely without the surrounding system.

A full PKI has several moving parts beyond the certificate authority covered in the previous chapter. Registration authorities often handle the identity verification legwork on behalf of a CA, so the CA itself can focus on signing rather than processing paperwork. Certificate repositories store and distribute issued certificates so relying parties can look them up. And critically, PKI has to account for the fact that certificates sometimes need to stop being trusted before their stated expiration date, if a private key is stolen or an organization changes hands. Certificate Revocation Lists, published periodically by CAs, list certificates that have been revoked early, and the Online Certificate Status Protocol lets a relying party query a CA in real time to check whether a specific certificate is still valid, rather than downloading an entire revocation list.

The everyday example nearly everyone touches without noticing is HTTPS. Every time a browser connects to a website over HTTPS, it is relying on the full PKI apparatus: a certificate authority verified the site's identity at some point, the site's certificate chains up to a root the browser trusts, and the browser optionally checks revocation status before completing the connection and encrypting the session. None of that infrastructure is visible to a typical user beyond a small padlock icon, which is exactly the point; PKI is meant to make identity-bound trust an invisible, automatic background process rather than something a person manually verifies for every connection.

It is worth noting, especially in a book about blockchain, that the two technologies take almost opposite approaches to trust. PKI ties every key to a verified real-world identity through a hierarchy of trusted authorities, which provides strong accountability but concentrates trust in those authorities, as the DigiNotar episode illustrated. Public blockchains like Bitcoin deliberately have no PKI at all: anyone can generate an address with no identity check, no registration authority, and no possibility of revocation, trading accountability for permissionless, unmediated access. Neither approach is simply better; they optimize for different things, and understanding PKI clearly is what makes that tradeoff visible rather than assumed.
